source_note: Public show notes and articles only (I cannot listen to audio). Points are paraphrased. Rask is an opinion source and most pages carry sponsorship or product promotion.
themes: Decide what the money is for and your growth vs safer split first; choosing the ETF comes after.
More ETFs do not mean more diversification: many hold the same big companies. Know the job each fund does.
Invest regularly and keep costs low rather than trying to time crashes (their own claim that markets rise in most years is unverified).
Brokerage and repeated trading quietly eat returns.
Set rules for how you will behave in falls before they happen; separate what you can control from what you cannot.

items.title: How to build a simple investment portfolio that actually works
points: Start with the purpose of the money, then split it between shares, bonds, cash and property.
Holding more funds does not automatically diversify you; overlapping ETFs are common.
Know your risk tolerance (how much you can stomach) and your risk capacity (how much you can afford to lose).
Let tax inform decisions but not drive them; set guardrails before markets get volatile.
items.promo: Sponsored by Global X; Pearler referral code and Rask product links.

items.title: How to build an ETF portfolio from scratch (Portfolio Construction, ep 1)
items.format: Podcast show notes (guest from fund issuer Global X)
points: Give every fund a job: a core holding plus smaller satellite holdings.
Overall allocation matters more than small differences between similar ETFs.
Watch for home bias and duplicated exposure.
Spreads, brokerage and frequent trading erode returns over time.
items.promo: Guest works for a fund issuer; sponsored by Global X.

items.title: Save like a pessimist, invest like an optimist
points: Focus on what you control: spending, savings rate, debt, how you invest, how you react.
Markets fall regularly; the author argues long-term investors have usually been rewarded (his 80%-of-years figure is not verified).
Invest regularly and diversify cheaply rather than predicting corrections.
Keep an emergency buffer and cut expensive debt before investing.
items.promo: Moderate: free-account, course and trial offers.

items.title: How many ETFs do you actually need?
points: Ask why you own each holding.
Different ETFs often hold the same large companies, so more funds can mean less diversification.
Set growth vs defensive allocation before picking ETFs.
Before buying another, check what it adds and why you are buying now.
items.promo: Moderate: Rask planning and trial offers; no issuer sponsor shown.

items.title: Why portfolio construction matters more than stock picking
points: A small number of stocks drive most market returns, which makes picking winners hard.
Research cited (not verified here) says most active managers trail their benchmark over the long run.
Decide the mix of Australian, global, bonds and gold before individual stocks.
ETFs let most people diversify without being stock-pickers.
items.promo: Explicit: sponsored by Global X ETFs.

items.title: The $6.7 trillion AI buildout: megatrend investing
items.format: Podcast show notes (guest from Global X)
points: The guest expects AI spending to flow to data centres, chips, power and some commodities.
She argues AI differs from the dot-com bubble because revenue already exists (her view, not a valuation call).
The top 10 companies are about 40% of the S&P 500, so broad funds already carry a lot of AI exposure.
Add theme funds carefully to avoid piling into the same companies.
items.promo: Explicit: sponsored by Global X and the guest works there.

items.title: AI's pricing reset: the unit economics investors cannot ignore
points: Per-seat software pricing may shrink if AI makes staff more productive.
Judge how much it costs to deliver each AI outcome.
"Recurring revenue" alone is not enough; ask what drives spending and how costs scale.
Look for pricing power and whether a company keeps the value it creates.

items.title: Debt recycling explained: how it works, traps and risks
points: How loans are split and used changes whether the interest is deductible.
What qualifies depends on structure and records; get an adviser and accountant first.
Compares gradual investing with a lump sum and asks if you could cope with falls while a loan remains.
Rate rises and cash-flow stress are the key risks.
items.promo: Pearler, PocketSmith and VanEck links plus Rask product links.

items.title: Is FIRE still a thing? A FIRE-proof ASX portfolio
points: The description lists a portfolio of three ETFs and two shares and the maths of how much is needed to retire early; the actual advice is not in the notes.

items.title: 4 steps to dollar-cost average into an ETF portfolio
points: Invest a fixed amount at set intervals to reduce timing risk, and stay invested.
Automate contributions so you keep going whatever the market does.
Timing buys after quarterly distributions can reduce brokerage.
Its worked example has a small arithmetic slip in the average price.
items.promo: Heavy: promotes Rask Invest's own account and fees; not a neutral how-to.
